strengths: Addresses a practical real-world problem (unified music restoration/mastering) with a single-pass generative model rather than cascaded task-specific tools

Comprehensive dataset contribution: 25k high-quality segments with 175k degraded variants across 19 effects in 5 categories, balanced by genre, with natural language annotations—valuable resource for future research

Artifact-aware evaluation metrics thoughtfully tailored to each degradation type (spectral balance, modulation spectra for reverb, etc.) with rigorous experimental protocol including objective metrics and subjective listening study
Text-controllable restoration via natural language prompts provides intuitive user control and creative flexibility beyond parameter tuning
Flow-matching approach correctly formulated with well-justified design choices (skewed time distribution emphasizing degraded inputs, velocity prediction in latent space)
Honest and transparent limitations discussion acknowledging VAE codec artifacts, full-song performance issues, and reverb evaluation challenges, demonstrating scientific integrity
Strong reproducibility commitment (code, model, dataset, samples, demo promised) with sufficient implementation details
Clear presentation with high-quality spectrograms and comprehensive appendix documenting degradation functions, prompts, and dataset construction pipeline
weaknesses: Significant performance degradation on full-song evaluation: Reverb metrics worsen substantially (e.g., Real RIR 0.3109→0.4066 in Table 2), undermining the practical applicability for mastering full tracks; crude linear interpolation for segment blending without exploration of alternatives

VAE latent codec introduces perceptible artifacts (reconstructed input FAD 0.139 vs. degraded 0.061), causing 'robotic' vocals and muted instruments especially for certain genres; model must overcome these artifacts rather than directly solve restoration task

Limited technical novelty: Flow-matching, Multimodal DiT, and FLAN-T5 conditioning are all existing techniques; architecture choices (6 MM-DiT + 18 DiT blocks, 10-sec audio conditioning) lack justification; main contribution is problem formulation and dataset rather than methodology

Weak baseline comparisons: Text2FX tested only for EQ single-task, WPE/HPSS are signal-processing methods from 2010+; no comparison with recent neural music restoration systems or cascaded pipelines of specialized tools; unclear whether SonicMaster outperforms well-engineered alternatives

Reverb evaluation acknowledged as problematic—authors state 'way a generative model removes reverb is not telegraphed, making metric selection difficult'; Euclidean distance on modulation spectra reliability on dense mixes is questionable

Small subjective listening study: 8 listeners evaluating 43 pairs with non-negligible confidence intervals (e.g., Preference 4.84±0.49); no inter-rater reliability metrics reported; limited statistical rigor beyond single paired t-test

Incomplete ablation analysis: Euler vs. Runge-Kutta results mixed without clear guidance on solver selection; audio conditioning length variations (5/10/15 sec) show minimal differences suggesting potential over-engineering

Dataset limited to Jamendo Creative Commons music (potential genre/production bias) with simulated rather than real-world degradations; transfer to out-of-distribution artifacts (extreme clipping, unusual rooms) not evaluated
Missing error analysis: No discussion of failure cases, which degradations/genres prove difficult, or which prompt formulations are most effective
SSIM metric shows counterintuitive results (SonicMaster SSIM 0.624 vs. degraded 0.838) contradicting listener preferences, suggesting SSIM poorly captures restoration task for audio

strengths: Well-motivated unified approach: Combining disparate audio restoration tasks (EQ, reverb, declipping, dynamics, stereo) in a single generative model is practically useful and avoids error propagation from cascaded specialized tools.

Valuable dataset contribution: The SonicMaster dataset of 175k degraded-clean audio pairs with natural-language prompts and 19 degradation functions across 10 genres could be useful for the community.
Comprehensive scope of degradations: 19 degradation functions spanning 5 categories with detailed specifications (Tables 6-8) provide clear documentation and reproducible degradation parameters.
Technically sound methodology: Flow-matching formulation and architecture combining Multimodal DiT with DiT blocks are well-executed; training procedure with classifier-free guidance is appropriate.
Multi-faceted evaluation approach: Objective metrics (FAD, KL, SSIM, PQ), degradation-specific metrics, and subjective listening study provide evaluation breadth.
Genre diversity: Careful curation across 10 genre groups with production quality filtering shows attention to dataset balance.
weaknesses: Critical evaluation gap—entirely synthetic data: All training and evaluation uses simulated degradations from synthetic reverbs (Pyroomacoustics), parametric EQs, and clipping models. There is zero evaluation on real-world degraded recordings from amateur productions, which is the stated use case. This undermines the core claim of being a 'restoration' system.

Paradoxical metric results inadequately explained: Standard metrics degrade—FAD increases (0.087→0.095) and SSIM drops (0.834→0.380) from degraded input to SonicMaster output on full songs. The paper attributes this to VAE codec artifacts ('robotic' vocals, muted instruments) but does not quantify, investigate, or resolve this contradiction, leaving fundamental doubts about output quality.

Underpowered listening study: Only 8 listeners (5 music experts, 3 MIR researchers) and 43 samples. No inter-rater reliability metrics (ICC/Fleiss' kappa) reported. Confidence intervals are wide; statistical power is insufficient to support preference claims. No comparison to alternative systems in subjective tests.

Weak baseline comparisons: Text2FX compared only for EQ (one category); WPE and HPSS are classical signal processing methods. Missing comparisons to recent music enhancement systems, diffusion-based audio editing methods, or modern deep learning alternatives. VoiceFixer mentioned but dismissed without empirical comparison.

No generalization evaluation: All testing on same dataset distribution (held-out test set). No cross-dataset validation, no real-world recordings, no evaluation of transfer from synthetic to real degradations. Synthetic-to-real generalization gap is completely unexplored.

Incomplete design ablations: No ablation on VAE codec choice despite acknowledged 'robotic' artifacts; no justification for Euler 10-step inference; audio pooling branch frequency (25%) unexplained; timestep distribution weighting (Eq. 2: 0.5U(t)+0.5t) lacks justification.

Full-song performance inconsistencies: Table 2 shows mixed (sometimes degraded) reverb metrics on full songs. Segment stitching via linear interpolation over 10s is crude; the paper acknowledges this limitation but does not propose or test solutions.

Text conditioning effectiveness unclear: Without text prompts, models achieve similar FAD (0.069 unchanged) and only modest KL degradation. Text conditioning benefit is marginal for several restoration categories (Reverb, Amplitude), undermining the central text-guided narrative.

Dataset filtering concerns: Only 4.3% (25k/580k) retention rate raises questions about selectivity. Quality filtering uses Audiobox Aesthetics (a neural model), introducing potential circularity and bias. Adaptive thresholds (6.5–8) across genres lack uniform justification.

Missing failure analysis: Paper acknowledges 'robotic' vocals and muted instruments as limitations but provides no quantitative measurement of frequency/severity, no systematic analysis of which degradations trigger artifacts, and no failure case examples or discussion.

Insufficient reproducibility: Code, model, and dataset stated as 'available' but not provided in submission. Sparse training hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, optimizer updates missing). VAE codec configuration underspecified.

Evaluation metrics misalignment: SSIM on mel-spectrograms known to be perceptually misaligned; results worsen despite claimed improvements. FAD/KL on CLAP embeddings for synthetic artifact restoration unvalidated. PQ score is external tool without independent interpretability.

No real-world validation whatsoever: Despite framing as a 'restoration and mastering' system for amateur recordings, there are zero experiments on actual amateur productions with authentic degradations. This is a critical gap for practical applicability claims.

Limited statistical rigor: No significance tests on objective metrics; confidence intervals only for listening study; no inter-rater reliability coefficients; sample selection methodology for listening study not clearly described.

Overstatement of contributions: Claims of 'professional-grade improvements' and 'fine-grained creative control' are not adequately supported given evaluation limitations. Synergy of unified approach over cascades not empirically demonstrated.

strengths: Novel unified framework addressing music restoration and mastering in a single generative model, with practical significance for amateur music producers
High-quality dataset contribution with 25k segments, 19 degradation types across 5 categories, 175k audio-text pairs, and comprehensive metadata—valuable resource for future research
Comprehensive evaluation combining objective metrics (FAD, KL, SSIM, PQ), degradation-specific artifact metrics, and subjective listening tests with proper experimental setup
Technically sound approach using rectified flow for direct degraded→clean mapping with appropriate multimodal conditioning (text via FLAN-T5 and audio via VAE codec)
Extensive ablation studies examining architecture variants, audio conditioning strategies, and inference methods with transparent experimental design
Strong commitment to reproducibility with promised release of code, model, dataset, and demo
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement, good figures, and comprehensive appendix documentation
weaknesses: Critical performance degradation on full songs: reverb metrics worsen (0.3667→0.3954), SSIM and FAD decrease for full-length audio, undermining practical applicability for the core use case despite acknowledgment
Evaluation limited to synthetic degradations only with no validation on real amateur recordings, creating substantial domain gap and questioning real-world generalization

Subjective listening study undersized for ICML main track: only 8 listeners on 43 sample pairs falls below community standards (typically ≥20 listeners); wide confidence intervals (e.g., EQ: 5.11±0.55)

VAE codec artifacts inadequately addressed: reconstructed baseline performs worse than degraded input in many metrics; paper acknowledges 'robotic vocals' and 'muted instruments' but provides no quantification, examples, or investigation of alternative encodings

Weak evidence for text conditioning effectiveness: model without text shows comparable or better performance on several metrics (FAD: 0.073 with text vs 0.069 without); no systematic study of prompt variations or robustness
Full-song segment stitching uses simplistic linear interpolation over 10-second overlap without exploring alternatives; no investigation of why performance degrades or solutions beyond speculation

Multiple arbitrary design choices without sufficient justification: pooled audio branch at 25% training rate, 15% hidden clipping injection, specific skewed time distribution, not compared against alternatives

Weak baseline comparisons: Text2FX hyperparameter tuning details unclear; no recent deep learning restoration models included; traditional methods (WPE, HPSS) not directly comparable to generative approach
Acknowledged metric limitations (RT60 unreliable on dense mixes, reverb evaluation challenging on polyphonic music) without proposing solutions, weakening evaluation validity
Missing practical considerations: no inference time reported, GPU memory requirements unspecified, automatic mode performance not thoroughly evaluated, real-time capability unclear

strengths: Well-motivated unified approach to multi-task music restoration avoiding cascading error from sequential task-specific modules

Comprehensive and systematic dataset construction: 25k high-quality Jamendo segments balanced across 10 genres with 19 degradation functions and natural language annotations; promised community release
Strong empirical results with 98.5% listener preference over Mel2Mel+Diffwave on reverb tasks and significant objective metric improvements across degradation categories

Thorough experimental evaluation including multiple objective metrics (FAD, KL, SSIM, PQ), subjective listening studies with expert listeners, ablation studies on architecture variants and conditioning strategies, and out-of-domain testing on piano recordings
Practical system design with text-conditioned control for fine-grained user guidance while maintaining automatic operation mode
Reasonable zero-shot generalization to out-of-domain historical recordings (PQ: 6.93 vs BABE-2's 7.05)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies existing techniques (flow matching from Liu et al. 2022/Esser et al. 2024, MM-DiT blocks from Esser et al. 2024, FLAN-T5 embeddings) primarily as engineering contribution rather than algorithmic innovation

Critical practical limitation inadequately addressed: full-song performance degrades significantly compared to 30s snippets, with reverb metrics often worse than degraded input (e.g., Big room 0.4511 vs 0.3654); proposed linear interpolation solution is ad-hoc and doesn't resolve the fundamental issue

Evaluation limitations: (1) weak baselines—most comparisons against trivial baselines or task-specific methods rather than general restoration approaches; only one general baseline (Mel2Mel+DiffWave); (2) small subjective studies (8 listeners for main study, 13 for comparative); (3) acknowledged metric unreliability for reverb (RT60 estimates) yet reverb evaluated with surrogate modulation spectrum metrics

Latent space artifacts inadequately characterized: paper acknowledges 'robotic vocals or muted instruments especially in certain genres' but provides no systematic analysis, examples, affected genres, or severity assessment

Text prompt robustness unexplored: all 8-10 prompts per degradation are hand-crafted; no study of paraphrase robustness or out-of-distribution prompts; no user study comparing expert-written vs. user-written prompts; critical gap for system emphasizing 'precise user control'

Reproducibility concerns: model/demo availability unclear (URL appears cut off), dataset release timeline not specified, code availability not mentioned, some training hyperparameters missing (learning rate, optimizer details)

Limited generalization validation: only piano recordings tested for out-of-domain evaluation; no assessment on speech-heavy, extreme amateur, non-Western, or live recordings; Jamendo dataset has Western music biases
Confusing architecture scaling results: SonicMasterMedium(6/6) performs worse than smaller variants with no explanation; contradicts technical clarity
Counterintuitive reconstructed input baselines: sometimes worse than degraded input (Tables 1-3), suggesting potential VAE or metric issues not adequately explained

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated problem scope: unifying multiple audio restoration tasks (19 degradations across 5 categories) is practically useful for non-expert users.

Systematic and well-documented dataset construction: 175k paired audio clips with carefully implemented degradation functions, detailed metadata, and natural language annotations provide a useful resource for the community.

Thorough experimental evaluation: multiple evaluation axes including objective metrics across degradation categories, subjective listening tests with both MOS and preference ratings, ablation studies, and out-of-domain generalization test on piano recordings.
Clear presentation and reproducible details: good documentation of degradation functions, prompts, ablations on ODE solvers, and architectural choices. Comprehensive appendices support transparency.
Reasonable architectural choices: the hybrid MM-DiT + DiT design with rectified flow is well-suited for the task, and ablations validate design decisions.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the architecture straightforwardly combines existing components (rectified flow from Liu et al. 2022, MM-DiT from Esser et al. 2024, FLAN-T5). No new algorithms, loss functions, or architectural innovations are introduced—this is primarily an engineering contribution.

Weak baseline comparisons: WPE/HPSS (2010) are classical methods; Mel2Mel + DiffWave (2022) is the only recent baseline. Text2FX comparison limited to EQ only. VoiceFixer (mentioned as related work) is never empirically compared. Missing comparisons with recent 2024-2025 audio enhancement methods.

Fundamental dataset limitation: all degradations are synthetically simulated using standard effects. Real-world audio quality issues have different statistical properties. No real degraded recordings. This undermines claims about practical applicability.

Severe performance degradation on full-length songs: Table 3 shows SSIM drops from ~0.62 (snippets) to ~0.38 (full songs)—a major regression. Full-song reverb metrics degrade compared to snippets. Authors acknowledge this is due to segment connection but provide no solution, severely limiting practical deployment.

Insufficient ablation of text conditioning value: removing text only significantly harms Clip (2.812 vs 1.506) and some other metrics; many remain similar. Only 10% text dropout tested (conservative). Unclear what proportion of improvements come from text vs. automatic restoration or which task types benefit from text guidance.

Questionable practical advantages over specialized methods: on piano recordings (out-of-domain), SonicMaster (PQ=6.93) does not beat BABE-2 (PQ=7.05), a specialized method. Coming close to a specialized approach doesn't justify replacing pipelines of tools. No computational cost (inference time, memory, energy) analysis provided.

Evaluation methodology concerns: reverb measured by proxy (modulation spectra distance) because RT60 is unreliable; unclear if proxy metrics correlate with perceptual quality. Subjective studies are small (8 listeners main study, 13 comparative). Clipping and stereo metrics are also indirect proxies.
Model and code availability unclear: abstract states 'available through' with no completion. No code release mentioned. No clear plan for dataset release. This undermines reproducibility claims.

Overstated claims and presentation issues: 'first unified generative model' is true but with limited novelty; 'significantly improves' mischaracterizes often modest gains. LLM was used to edit paper for space (Section A.1), raising academic integrity concerns.

Missing practical analysis: no inference latency measurements compared to alternatives; no parameter count comparisons; SonicMaster_Small nearly matches SonicMaster_Large performance, questioning whether the large model is necessary. Scaling is inefficient.

strengths: Novel unified approach to music restoration and mastering addressing 19 degradation types across 5 categories in a single text-guided generative model—genuinely the first of its kind
Well-curated SonicMaster dataset (25k high-quality segments, 175k paired degraded-clean samples with metadata and natural language annotations) that will be valuable for the research community

Comprehensive experimental evaluation combining multiple objective metrics (FAD, KL, SSIM, PQ, degradation-specific measures), subjective listening studies (8 experts + 13 comparative participants), ablation studies, and out-of-domain generalization tests

Strong empirical results with overwhelming listener preferences: 98.5% preference over Mel2Mel+DiffWave for reverb and 93.8% for EQ across 130 comparisons, plus competitive performance on piano recordings (PQ 6.93 vs. BABE-2's 7.05)

Technically sound methodology with well-motivated architectural choices (rectified flow for direct degraded-to-clean mapping, hybrid MM-DiT+DiT design, latent-space restoration avoiding computational overhead)
Good reproducibility with detailed training specifications, comprehensive appendix documenting degradations and prompts, inference procedures well-documented, and dataset to be released
Clear presentation of well-motivated practical problem—amateur recordings require multi-stage manual restoration that non-experts cannot effectively perform
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in components: MM-DiT, DiT, rectified flow, VAE, and FLAN-T5 are all existing; main contribution is application and integration rather than methodological innovation

Synthetic degradation gap: all 19 degradations are deterministic simulations (parametric EQ, room impulse responses, compression algorithms) that may not capture real-world complexity; only tested on old piano recordings and Jamendo-sourced data, not truly realistic amateur recordings with natural multi-source degradations

Mixed and unexplained full-song results: reverberation performance degrades on full songs compared to 30s snippets (0.3109→0.4066 for Real reverb) with only vague explanation about 'increased complexity'; fundamental limitation unresolved

Inconsistent architecture scaling: SonicMasterMedium (6MM-DiT/6DiT) performs worst across all metrics with no satisfactory explanation, suggesting potential training dynamics issues or architectural incompleteness

Small and narrow subjective evaluation: first listening study uses only 8 listeners (5 experts + 3 MIR researchers) with limited demographic diversity; second study 13 participants on 20 samples from authors' curated test set; no real-world amateur recording evaluation

Shallow text conditioning analysis: improvements are sometimes modest, counterintuitive finding that no-conditioning achieves optimal Boom correction (suggesting text sometimes interferes), no sensitivity analysis for prompt variations, no investigation of which prompts work well vs. poorly

Missing critical analyses: no computational cost (inference time/memory), no failure case analysis, limited classifier-free guidance ablations, insufficient investigation of pooled audio branch design, no visualization of learned text embeddings or restoration trajectories

Circular evaluation: test set drawn from same Jamendo dataset used for training; no held-out real-world validation; baseline comparisons limited (Text2FX only for EQ, no BABE-2 comparison on full restoration, no comparison with recent specialized methods)

Incomplete disclosure: 'model and demo samples are available through [incomplete]'—unclear whether code will be released; ethics/licensing discussion minimal; no discussion of misuse potential; use of LLM for paper compression noted but implications unclear
